Renato, I have the review here. Before I redraw anything, tell me in your own words where the problem is.
The problem is not the size of the territory. It is the workload. My people in the Southeast carry almost twice as many accounts as the ones in the South.
And that shows up in the numbers?
It does. Coverage in the South is better than in the Southeast, ninety-one against eighty-four. The benchmark is one visit a month for every key account, and we are missing it in the interior.
Where exactly is the worst part? I need one place, not a state.
The interior of Sao Paulo. Reach is lowest there and the backlog is the longest we have. One more position would close the biggest gap in the country.
Good. Headquarters has approved one position, so we can split the territory. How do you want the two consultants there to be ranked?
Coverage first, growth second, and the backlog they inherited third. And I want to speak to each of them alone before anything is announced.
That last part is the one most managers skip. Send me the criteria in writing and I will allocate the new position this week.

People think we draw territories with a ruler, and we do not. If you split a country by area, you get one consultant with a beautiful map and no clients, and another one drowning in a city block. So we start from the other end. We count the clients who actually buy, we weight them, and only then do we draw the line. The second thing nobody expects is that the biggest territory is almost never the best one. The best territory is the one where the workload matches the person. I have seen a consultant lose half a region because somebody gave them more accounts than any human being can visit in a month. And the last thing. Every time we redraw a map, somebody loses a client they have known for six years. That part is not a spreadsheet problem, and if a manager treats it like one, the redraw fails, no matter how good the numbers look.

Two years ago I split my largest territory in half, and I got the sequence completely wrong. I announced the new maps on a Monday morning, in a group call, with the numbers on a slide. It was efficient and it was a disaster. Two of my best people spent the rest of the quarter wondering what the decision said about them. What I would do differently is simple, and it costs nothing. Talk to each person alone, before the group call, and tell them the reason first and the map second. The reason is almost always coverage. Nobody argues with the idea that a client who is visited twice a year is a client we are going to lose. What people argue with is a map that appears on a screen with no explanation attached to it. The split itself was right. We reached more clients that year than the year before, with the same headcount. It was the way I told the story that cost me two quarters of trust.

The Southeast is our largest territory, and it is more complex than the South. We allocate four consultants to it, because the workload there is heavier. The South is smaller, but the coverage is better than it was last year. Our benchmark is simple: every key account is visited at least once a month.
